title: What C++20 and C++23 Add
summary: Build C++20 in the sandbox: concepts, ranges, span, defaulted comparisons, designated initializers, consteval, and coroutines, with C++23 shown on a Mac.
intro: The sandbox runs C++17 on g++ 10.2, and so does a lot of production code, which is why this course is written in it. The newer standards keep everything you've learned and add shorter, safer ways to say the same things. The sandbox builds a file as C++20 when its first line is `// -std=c++20`, the way `g++ -std=c++20` would in a terminal, so most of this lesson runs for real there. On your Mac, `clang++ -std=c++20` does the same. g++ 10.2 has most of C++20's language but not all of its library, and none of C++23, so `std::format`, `std::print`, `std::expected`, and modules come from Apple clang 21 on a Mac, with the output it printed. MSVC takes `/std:c++20` or `/std:c++latest`. Each part says which C++17 lesson the new feature replaces.

steps.title: Concepts instead of enable_if

example.title: Concept-checked mid and price
example.prompt: Constrain mid with standard concepts and price with a Payoff concept of your own, then count calls in a constinit global and scale with a consteval function.
example.explanation:
Each `mid` call keeps the one template whose concept its argument type satisfies. `std::int64_t` and `int` are integral, so 10125 and 10126 give 10125, and 99 and 102 give 100. A `double` is floating point, so it gets the exact average. That's the `enable_if` pair of *Compile-Time C++: constexpr, static_assert, and Type Traits* with the trick gone.

`static_assert(!Payoff<Quote>)` passes, because calling a `Quote` doesn't compile and the concept tested that quietly. `g_priced` is `constinit`, so it's 0 before any code runs, and `price` still adds to it. `ten_to(8)` is `consteval`: it ran while compiling, and the program holds only the 100000000.

One quirk of this mode: g++ 10 still sets `__cplusplus` to 201709 rather than C++20's 202002, since its C++20 isn't complete, so a check like `#if __cplusplus >= 202002L` from *The Preprocessor: Macros and Conditional Compilation* fails here. Code that needs a feature tests that feature's own macro, like `__cpp_concepts`, instead.

practice.title: Grid checks and fees with concepts
practice.prompt:
Check prices against the tick grid and add up trading costs, with concepts doing the type checks.

1. Replace the starter's `is_on_grid` with two templates: one for `std::integral` types that returns `price % tick == 0`, and one for `std::floating_point` types that computes `const T steps = price / tick;` and returns `std::abs(steps - std::round(steps)) < 1e-9`.
2. Write the concept `Fee`: given a `const F& f`, an `int qty`, and a `double px`, `f(qty, px)` compiles and gives something convertible to `double`.
3. `static_assert` that `Flat` and `Bps` are Fees and that `Quote` isn't.
4. Finish `total_cost(fee, qty, px)`: `qty * px` plus the fee.
5. `main` reads an integer price and tick, a decimal price and tick, and a quantity and price, then prints the four lines shown.

Input:

```text
10125 5
101.27 0.05
100 101.25
```

Expected output:

```text
10125 on grid 5: true
101.27 on grid 0.05: false
flat: 10126.00
bps: 10129.05
```

tests.output:
10125 on grid 5: true
101.27 on grid 0.05: false
flat: 10126.00
bps: 10129.05

10126 on grid 5: false
101.25 on grid 0.05: true
flat: 1026.00
bps: 1025.41

200 on grid 25: true
0.3 on grid 0.1: true
flat: 1001.00
bps: 1000.40

hints: The two `is_on_grid` templates differ only in their first line, `template <std::integral T>` or `template <std::floating_point T>`, like the two `mid`s.
`Fee` reads like the example's `Payoff`, with `requires(const F& f, int qty, double px)` and one line for the call `f(qty, px)`.
`Bps{4.0}` charges 4 basis points: 10125 × 4 / 10000 is 4.05, so its total is 10129.05.

steps.title: Ranges, views, and std::span

example.title: Fills through ranges and spans
example.prompt: Sort fills with a projection, total a filtered and transformed view with no allocations, and pass slices of a vector as spans.
example.output:
NVDA 30 @ 13950
AAPL 100 @ 19275
AAPL 200 @ 19280
AAPL -40 @ 19290
MSFT -50 @ 41010
AAPL bought 300, allocations 0
sells 2, NVDA qty 30
notional 3379900, two cheapest 2346000, priciest -2050500
sizeof(span) 16
example.explanation:
`std::ranges::sort(fills, {}, &Fill::px)` compares the `px` of each pair, so the fills come out by price, cheapest first. `aapl_buys` is a view: building it ran nothing, and the loop pulled each fill through the filter, then through the transform, which reads the `qty` member, adding 100 and 200. The `operator new` at the top replaces the global one and counts every allocation, as in *`string_view` and Fast Parsing*, and the whole pipeline made none.

`std::ranges::find` with the projection `&Fill::symbol` looks for the fill whose symbol is `NVDA`. `notional` takes a `std::span<const Fill>`, so one function adds up all five fills, the first two, or the last one, with no copy and no template.

practice.title: Quotes through ranges and spans
practice.prompt:
Sort quotes, list the wide ones through a view, and find the widest spread through spans.

1. Sort `quotes` by `bid` with `std::ranges::sort` and a projection, and print each as `symbol bid ask`.
2. Make a view of the symbols of the quotes whose spread, `ask - bid`, is at least `min_spread`, with `std::views::filter` and `std::views::transform`. Print `wide:`, then each symbol after a space.
3. Finish `widest(quotes)`, which takes a `std::span<const Quote>`: the largest spread, or 0 for no quotes.
4. Print `widest `, the widest spread of all the quotes, then `, top two ` and the widest of the last two after sorting, the two highest bids.

The input is `n` and `min_spread`, then `n` quotes, at least two.

Input:

```text
4 5
MSFT 41005 41010
AAPL 19270 19280
NVDA 13940 13965
AAPL 19271 19272
```

Expected output:

```text
NVDA 13940 13965
AAPL 19270 19280
AAPL 19271 19272
MSFT 41005 41010
wide: NVDA AAPL MSFT
widest 25, top two 5
```

tests.output:
NVDA 13940 13965
AAPL 19270 19280
AAPL 19271 19272
MSFT 41005 41010
wide: NVDA AAPL MSFT
widest 25, top two 5

USDJPY 15012 15013
EURUSD 108340 108345
GBPUSD 126500 126502
wide: EURUSD GBPUSD
widest 5, top two 5

AAPL 19270 19280
MSFT 41005 41010
wide:
widest 10, top two 10

hints: Sorting by a member is `std::ranges::sort(quotes, {}, &Quote::bid);`, like the example's sort by `&Fill::px`.
The filter's lambda captures `min_spread`, `[min_spread](const Quote& q) { return q.ask - q.bid >= min_spread; }`, and the transform can be the member pointer `&Quote::symbol`.
Make `const std::span<const Quote> all(quotes);`, then call `widest(all)` and `widest(all.last(2))`.

steps.title: Comparisons, initializers, and format

example.title: Price levels that compare themselves
example.prompt: Order price levels with a defaulted spaceship operator, build them with designated initializers, then sort them and count the distinct ones.
example.output:
true false true true
19280 x 0
19275 x 300
19275 x 100
distinct 2
true true true
example.explanation:
`Level`'s defaulted `<=>` compares `px` first and `qty` second. So `a < b` is true at the same price because 100 is less than 300, `a != b` comes from the defaulted `==`, and `c` is greater than `b` on price alone. `std::greater{}` flips the order, so `std::ranges::sort` puts the best bid first. The set kept 2 of its 3 values, since the two copies of `a` compare equal.

`c` names only `px`, so its `qty` started at 0. `Quote` holds `double`s, so its `<=>` returns `std::partial_ordering`, while `Level`'s returns `std::strong_ordering`.

practice.title: Asks in price-time priority
practice.prompt:
Sort resting sell orders into price-time priority with a defaulted spaceship operator.

An exchange fills the cheapest ask first, and at the same price, the one that arrived first. Declare the fields in that order and the default comparison is exactly that rule.

1. Reorder `Ask`'s fields to `px`, `ts_ns`, then `qty`, and default `operator<=>`.
2. For each input line `px ts qty`, push an `Ask` built with designated initializers.
3. Sort the asks with `std::ranges::sort` and print each as `px ts qty`.
4. Print `at the best price: ` and how many asks share the first ask's price, using `std::ranges::count` with the projection `&Ask::px`.
5. Print `first two equal: ` and whether the first two asks are equal, as `true` or `false`.

The input is `n`, at least 2, then `n` asks.

Input:

```text
4
19280 1500 100
19275 1700 50
19280 1200 300
19275 1600 25
```

Expected output:

```text
19275 1600 25
19275 1700 50
19280 1200 300
19280 1500 100
at the best price: 2
first two equal: false
```

tests.output:
41005 950 20
41005 950 20
41010 900 10
at the best price: 2
first two equal: true

13950 100 5
13955 50 5
at the best price: 1
first two equal: false

hints: The defaulted `<=>` compares fields top to bottom, so `px` must come first and `ts_ns` second.
Build each one as `Ask{.px = px, .ts_ns = ts, .qty = qty}`, with the names in declaration order.
`std::ranges::count(asks, asks.front().px, &Ask::px)` counts the asks whose `px` equals the best one.

steps.title: Coroutines, expected, and modules

example.title: Cutting fields with a generator
example.prompt: Write a coroutine that yields the fields of a FIX-style message one at a time, stop pulling once the price arrives, and count the heap allocations.
example.explanation:
Calling `fields` runs none of its body: `initial_suspend` pauses it at once and hands back the `Generator`. Each `next()` resumes it until the next `co_yield`, which stores one field in the promise and pauses again, with `msg` and `bar` kept in between. The loop stops after `44=19275`, so `38=100` is never cut out, the laziness a vector of fields can't give you. For the heartbeat, the body reaches `co_return`, `done()` turns true, and `next()` returns false after the third field.

The paused locals live in a *coroutine frame* that `new` allocates, one per generator, which the replaced `operator new` counts: 1, then 2. g++ 10.2 allocates it even at `-O2`. Apple clang at `-O2` removed it for this program, since each generator dies in the function that made it, but don't count on that. Make generators where a program starts up, not once per message. The first line, `// -std=c++20 -fcoroutines`, is what g++ 10 needs for coroutines.

practice.title: A price grid generator
practice.prompt:
Write an endless generator of price levels and pull levels from it until one reaches a target.

1. The starter has the example's `Generator` unchanged. Write the coroutine `levels(start, tick)`, which yields `start`, `start + tick`, `start + 2 * tick`, and so on, forever.
2. In `main`, pull levels with `next()` and print each one on its own line, stopping after the first level at or above `target`.
3. Print `levels ` and how many levels you printed.

The input is `start`, `tick`, and `target`, with `tick` above 0.

Input:

```text
19270 5 19290
```

Expected output:

```text
19270
19275
19280
19285
19290
levels 5
```
hints: A loop with no end condition is fine in a coroutine, since the caller decides how many values to pull: `for (std::int64_t px = start;; px += tick) { co_yield px; }`.
The loop in `main` is the example's: `while (grid.next()) { ... }`, with a `break` once `grid.value() >= target`.
Print and count the level before checking the target, so the level that reaches it is printed too.

recap:
- A first line of `// -std=c++20` builds the sandbox file as C++20, plus `-fcoroutines` for coroutines. `clang++ -std=c++20` does it on a Mac.
- Concepts replace `enable_if`: `template <std::integral T>`, or your own `concept Payoff = requires(...) { ... };`. A failed concept is reported at the call, with the requirement that failed.
- `consteval` must run while compiling. `constinit` makes a global's first value a compile-time one and leaves it changeable.
- `std::ranges::sort(v, {}, &T::member)` takes the container and a projection. Views like `std::views::filter` and `std::views::transform` chain with `|`, run lazily, and allocate nothing.
- `std::span<const T>` is a pointer and a length over any contiguous elements: vectors, `std::array`s, plain arrays. It dangles like a `string_view`.
- `auto operator<=>(const T&) const = default;` gives all six comparisons, member by member in declaration order.
- Designated initializers, `T{.a = 1, .b = 2}`, name the fields in declaration order and value-initialize the rest.
- A coroutine pauses at `co_yield` and resumes on demand. g++ 10.2 allocates its frame on the heap, so make generators off the hot path.
- Past g++ 10.2: `std::format` and `std::print` replace iomanip, `std::expected` replaces the `Result` you built, and modules replace headers. `std::jthread` is in g++ 10.2 already.

Next, **Coroutines in Depth: Awaitables, Tasks, and an Event Loop** opens up the machinery behind that generator, and builds tasks an event loop resumes as a feed delivers data.
